findings.explanation: The grant targets google_project_service_identity.bigquery, which resolves to service-<num>@gcp-sa-bigquery.iam.gserviceaccount.com. BigQuery does not use that identity for CMEK: encryption and decryption run as the separate BigQuery encryption service agent, bq-<num>@bigquery-encryption.iam.gserviceaccount.com, exposed by the data source google_bigquery_default_service_account (confirmed present in the google provider schema). Three resources depend on that key - the dataset's default_encryption_configuration, the connection's kms_key_name, and the transfer config's encryption_configuration - so the very first apply fails with a Cloud KMS permission denied on all of them. Every deterministic rule passes because a google_kms_crypto_key_iam_member granting cryptoKeyEncrypterDecrypter on the right key does exist; no rule can tell that the member is the wrong one of two similarly-named BigQuery service agents.
findings.remediation: Add `data "google_bigquery_default_service_account" "bigquery" {}` and point the grant's member at it. The google_project_service_identity.bigquery resource is then unused and can be removed.
findings.title: BigQuery CMEK key is granted to the wrong service identity, so no BigQuery resource can use it

findings.explanation: google_storage_bucket.landing sets logging.log_bucket to this bucket, but GCS delivers access logs as the group cloud-storage-analytics@google.com, which has no binding here. With uniform_bucket_level_access = true there is no legacy ACL fallback, so delivery fails silently: the apply succeeds, the config looks audited, and no log object is ever written. A rules engine sees a well-formed logging block on the source bucket and a compliant destination bucket, and has no way to check that the delivery principal was granted anything.
findings.remediation: Add a google_storage_bucket_iam_member granting roles/storage.objectCreator on the logging bucket to group:cloud-storage-analytics@google.com.
findings.title: Access logging is configured but the log-delivery principal cannot write to the destination bucket

findings.explanation: google_service_account.transfer is passed to the module as the identity the transfer runs as, and the module's connection_service_account output exists specifically to be granted access to whatever the connection reads. Neither receives a single IAM binding: the transfer SA has no storage.objectViewer on the landing bucket and no bigquery.dataEditor on the landing dataset, and the caller has no serviceAccountTokenCreator on it despite the README naming that as a requirement. The example therefore cannot run, and the usual reaction to the resulting permission errors is to attach a broad project-level role - which is exactly what the example should be steering people away from. No rule fires because absence of a binding is indistinguishable from a binding held elsewhere.
findings.remediation: Add narrowly-scoped bindings: roles/storage.objectViewer on google_storage_bucket.landing and roles/bigquery.dataEditor on google_bigquery_dataset.landing for google_service_account.transfer, plus roles/iam.serviceAccountTokenCreator for the applying principal.
findings.title: Example creates two service identities and grants neither anything, leaving least-privilege undemonstrated

findings.explanation: The member is built by string interpolation from the project number and a hardcoded gs-project-accounts.iam.gserviceaccount.com domain. The provider ships google_storage_project_service_account for exactly this, which returns the address Google actually uses and does not silently produce a valid-looking but wrong principal if the format ever changes. Principle is a best-fit: this is an apply-correctness footgun rather than a security gap per se.
findings.title: GCS service agent address is hand-constructed instead of read from its data source

suggested_policies.rationale: holden already has HLD_GCP_456 (GCS buckets/objects using CMEK must grant the GCS service agent key access) and HLD_GCP_466 for its ordering, but there is no BigQuery equivalent - coverage_by_type lists only HLD_GCP_399 and HLD_GCP_400 (both CMEK-present checks) for google_bigquery_connection and google_bigquery_data_transfer_config, and nothing on google_bigquery_dataset for the companion grant. The condition is a fixed resource type plus a required companion resource, the same shape HLD_GCP_456 already uses, so no DSL extension is needed. This is the exact defect found as HOLDEN_AI_001.
suggested_policies.yaml:
id: HLD_PROPOSED_001
name: BigQuery resources using CMEK must grant the BigQuery encryption service agent key access
principle: key-management
severity: HIGH
rationale: |
  BigQuery encrypts and decrypts CMEK-protected datasets, tables, connections
  and transfer configs as a dedicated service agent,
  bq-<PROJECT_NUMBER>@bigquery-encryption.iam.gserviceaccount.com, exposed by the
  google_bigquery_default_service_account data source. This is a different
  identity from service-<PROJECT_NUMBER>@gcp-sa-bigquery.iam.gserviceaccount.com,
  which google_project_service_identity returns for bigquery.googleapis.com.
  Granting the key to the wrong one looks correct and passes every
  attribute-level check, but the first apply fails with Cloud KMS permission
  denied.
remediation: |
  Grant the BigQuery encryption service agent access to the key:

    data "google_bigquery_default_service_account" "bigquery" {}

    resource "google_kms_crypto_key_iam_member" "bigquery_cmek" {
      crypto_key_id = google_kms_crypto_key.example.id
      role          = "roles/cloudkms.cryptoKeyEncrypterDecrypter"
      member        = "serviceAccount:${data.google_bigquery_default_service_account.bigquery.email}"
    }
resources:
  google_bigquery_dataset:
    path: default_encryption_configuration.kms_key_name
    requires_companion:
      type: google_kms_crypto_key_iam_member
      path: member
      contains: bigquery-encryption.iam.gserviceaccount.com

suggested_policies.dsl_extension_note: Needs a two-hop check that the existing DSL cannot express: resolve a reference from resource A (google_storage_bucket.logging.log_bucket) to resource B (another google_storage_bucket), then assert a requires_companion condition against B rather than against A. Today `references.must` accepts only a leaf attribute condition on the target, and `requires_companion` only anchors on the resource the policy block is declared for. The primitive needed is allowing a companion-existence condition inside `references.must`, scoped so the companion's linking attribute (google_storage_bucket_iam_member.bucket) must resolve to B's name.
suggested_policies.rationale: A bucket that names a log_bucket looks fully compliant to every existing rule, but GCS writes access logs as group:cloud-storage-analytics@google.com and delivery fails silently when that principal has no objectCreator binding on the destination - especially under uniform bucket-level access, where there is no legacy ACL fallback. coverage_by_type for google_storage_bucket lists fourteen policies, including HLD_GCP_003 (logging enabled) and HLD_GCP_451 (must not log to itself), none of which checks that the delivery principal can write. This is HOLDEN_AI_002.
suggested_policies.yaml:
id: HLD_PROPOSED_002
name: GCS access-log destination buckets must grant the log delivery principal write access
principle: logging-and-monitoring
severity: MEDIUM
rationale: |
  Cloud Storage delivers usage and storage logs as the group
  cloud-storage-analytics@google.com. If that principal holds no write role on
  the bucket named in logging.log_bucket, delivery fails silently: the apply
  succeeds, the source bucket appears to have audit logging enabled, and no log
  object is ever written. Uniform bucket-level access removes the legacy ACL
  fallback that used to mask this.
remediation: |
  Grant the delivery group objectCreator on the destination bucket:

    resource "google_storage_bucket_iam_member" "log_delivery" {
      bucket = google_storage_bucket.logs.name
      role   = "roles/storage.objectCreator"
      member = "group:cloud-storage-analytics@google.com"
    }
resources:
  google_storage_bucket:
    references:
      via: logging.log_bucket
      type: google_storage_bucket
      must:
        requires_companion:
          type: google_storage_bucket_iam_member
          path: member
          equals: "group:cloud-storage-analytics@google.com"
